subject: Estimating means of two multi variate normals

messages.author: 2e61a423209bab0c
messages.subject: Estimating means of two multi variate normals
parts:
Hello,

Could anyone explain to me why the code below 

data {
  int<lower=0> M; // M=10
  vector[M] Y[2]; // first column contains values close to 0, second column contains values close to 20 	
  vector[M] ones; // generated in R as ones = rep(1,M)
  matrix[M,M] Sigma; // generated in R as Sigma = diag(M)
}
parameters{
real mu1;
real mu2;
}
model{
Y[1] ~ multi_normal(mu1*ones,Sigma);
Y[2] ~ multi_normal(mu2*ones,Sigma);
}

gives me two chains, one for each mu, with a mean of about 10? I would expect a mean of 0 for the chain for mu1 and a mean of 20 for the chain for mu2. Indeed, when Y consists of only one column with values close to 20, I get a chain for mu with mean 20. Also, when I use 

parameters{
vector[M] mu1;
vector[M] mu2;
}
model{
Y[1] ~ multi_normal(mu1,Sigma);
Y[2] ~ multi_normal(mu2,Sigma);
}

instead, I get M chains for mu1 with means close to 0 and M chains for mu2 with means close to 20, which makes sense. I have attached the R code (also including the session info) and the model text file, in case that might be helpful.

Any help would be very much appreciated!

Rivka

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Estimating means of two multi variate normals
parts:
On Friday, November 9, 2012 2:50:25 PM UTC-5, Rivka wrote:
Could anyone explain to me why the code below 

data {
  int<lower=0> M; // M=10
  vector[M] Y[2]; // first column contains values close to 0, second column contains values close to 20 	
  vector[M] ones; // generated in R as ones = rep(1,M)
  matrix[M,M] Sigma; // generated in R as Sigma = diag(M)
}

The problem is that the input / output in Stan differs from that in R, and the input / output in Stan only makes sense if you think like a computer scientist. While in R

> Y
             [,1]     [,2]
 [1,] -0.08995044 20.04202
 [2,] -0.01903388 20.08355
 [3,] -0.12560167 19.94536
 [4,]  0.18268488 19.97778
 [5,]  0.19369427 19.90821
 [6,] -0.11684671 20.03746
 [7,] -0.04922991 19.98588
 [8,]  0.16634998 19.92019
 [9,] -0.07885807 20.07424
[10,]  0.08351772 20.07282


in Stan, this Y looks like

Y[1] = [-0.08995044, 20.04202, ..., 0.19369427, 19.90821]
Y[2] = [-0.11684671, 20.03746, ..., 0.08351772, 20.07282]

You could get the expected result if you transpose Y in R before passing it to Stan, like

myData <- list(Y=t(Y),M=M, ones=rep(1,M), Sigma = diag(M))

But it would be more transparent to write your .stan file in terms of a Y matrix instead of a collection of vectors, like

data {
  int<lower=0> M; 
  matrix[M,2] Y;	
  vector[M] ones;
  matrix[M,M] Sigma;
}
parameters{
  real mu1;
  real mu2;
}
model{
  col(Y,1) ~ multi_normal(mu1*ones,Sigma);
  col(Y,2) ~ multi_normal(mu2*ones,Sigma);
}

Finally, perhaps you are building toward a more complicated model where multi_normal() is actually necessary, but multi_normal() should only be used as a last resort because it is extremely slow. In this case with a diagonal Sigma, univariate normal models would suffice, like

data { int<lower=0> M; matrix[M,2] Y; } parameters{ real mu1; real mu2; } model{ col(Y,1) ~ normal(mu1,1.0); col(Y,2) ~ normal(mu2,1.0); }

Ben
